prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre that renews lyric, essay and narrative through the encounter between classical antiquity and modern experience, inventing hybrid forms of exposed feeling and intellectual daring

statement.case_for: My opening ranking stands. I rest the case on the work, not on the fact that every opening ranking put Carson first, since agreement among opening rankings is not evidence of merit. Her voice is recognisable in a few lines. She is also formally inventive in ways that serve emotional and intellectual ends, which the other shortlisted candidates do less consistently. Autobiography of Red turns the Geryon myth into a modern verse novel with real erotic and emotional exposure. Nox makes elegy for a brother into a made object that holds translation, philology, archive and grief together, so the form carries the mourning. These are not genre mixtures for their own sake. The same preoccupations (loss, desire, the limits of translation, the weight of the inherited past) run through the poetry, essays, verse drama and translations from Greek. That coherence across genres makes the whole oeuvre a single project, which a citation can name. Her handling of the relation between the living and the dead across time also fits the way a work can carry history and the present together. The ambition is serious: to renew what lyric and narrative can hold, in the direction of Nobel's will.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation concerns sustained breadth and weight. Much of the work is short, fragmentary or object-like, and some of its effect depends on typography, page design and layout that a citation or summary cannot capture. The classical allusiveness raises a fair question about where scholarship ends and literary achievement begins, and about how much her translations should count. If the committee judged that her best work is concentrated in a few books, or that the hybrid mode is more admired than durable, the case would weaken. Cărtărescu's scale of ambition and Zurita's moral and memorial weight are serious competing claims, and I cannot rule out that a close reading of the full corpus would favour one of them.

responses.point: Olsson finds it hard to isolate the core of Carson's achievement across so many genres, and notes that the list gives only two representative works, so any assessment of the whole oeuvre rests on general public knowledge.
responses.response: I agree that the range makes the core harder to isolate, and I share the caution about corpus coverage. My answer is that the core is the verse novel and the book-length elegy. Autobiography of Red and Nox are where the formal reinvention is fullest, and the essays, drama and translations show the same preoccupation from other angles. That is why I would not let the translations carry the citation, and I would keep the citation on her own writing. I take his point about only two named works as a real limit on what I can claim, and I do not claim to have verified the wider corpus.

responses.point: Mattson notes that Carson's effect depends heavily on typography, page design and allusion, so the work may travel unevenly in translation, and asks whether the scholar-poet hybrid fits Nobel's 'ideal direction' criterion.
responses.response: The translation risk is real, and it is larger for Carson than for most. I would qualify it, though. Her work comes with its own scaffolding: the myth in Autobiography of Red and the brother's loss in Nox are legible without the page design, and English is her original language, so the loss is in translation into Swedish and other languages, not in the original. On the 'ideal direction' question, I read the criterion as pointing to work of imaginative and intellectual depth that gives literature new possibilities. The hybrid is not a retreat into scholarship, because the scholarship is put at the service of emotional exposure. I accept that the committee could reasonably read it differently.

responses.point: Swärd finds Carson's allusiveness to Greek texts raises the question of how much weighs as literary achievement as distinct from scholarship, and says that would need close reading.
responses.response: I agree this needs close reading, and I would not settle it by assertion. The test I would apply is whether the classical material is the subject or the occasion. In Autobiography of Red the Stesichorus fragments are the occasion for a new love story with its own voice, so I read the achievement as literary. I also agree with her that the translation work should stay in the context and not carry the citation. Where we differ slightly is on Zurita. She ranks him second, and I think the landscape interventions are a harder claim to make for a literary prize, though I accept her view that they belong to the poetry and not to separate artworks.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu third and flags both translation losses from the density of his Romanian prose and some repetition of motifs, while keeping Carson first for formal invention serving emotional and intellectual ends.
responses.response: I share both worries about Cărtărescu, which is part of why I keep him second and not first. The repetition risk in the very long novels is real, and a prose whose force lies in sentence-level texture is more exposed to translation than Carson's, whose structures survive better. Where I would qualify her view is on durability: she says Cărtărescu's is probably good but untested, and I see the late phase, Solenoid in particular, as evidence of continued ambition. That keeps him a serious alternative. I would not move him ahead of Carson unless a closer reading of the Romanian original showed that the translations understate him.

uncertainties: How much weight Carson's translations from Greek and her classical scholarship should carry against her original writing is a judgment call, and I would keep them as context.
I have not independently verified her later publications, and my knowledge of recent work is incomplete.
Typography, layout and the book-object dimension of Nox and similar works cannot be fully judged from public descriptions.
Translation into Swedish and other languages may carry her allusive, page-dependent forms unevenly.
The shortlist gives only two representative works per writer, so claims about the whole oeuvre rest on general public knowledge and not on verified reading.
Whether a close reading of Cărtărescu in Romanian or Zurita in Spanish would change the ranking cannot be settled from translations.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records formal interests in ekphrasis, myth and fairy tale and a Lagerlöf biography. These are context about the member's own practice, not evidence of a preference or a reason for recusal.
